newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-FLORIDA TOWN WANTS TO APOLOGIZE TO ROBINSON.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-FLORIDA TOWN WANTS TO APOLOGIZE TO ROBINSON.

text.p: A Florida town that kicked Jackie Robinson off its baseball field 51 years ago said Wednesday it wanted to apologise to Robinson's family for what one city leader called "a stain ...on our soul."

In February of 1946 -- a year before Robinson became the first black player in major league baseball -- police in Sanford escorted Robinson off the field at Municipal Park rather than allow him to play in an exhibition game between the Montreal Royals and the Brooklyn Dodgers.

"The city of Sanford, much like most small towns in the south those days, had an ordinance that prohibited blacks and whites playing together on city-owned land," said Larry Dale, the current mayor of Sanford, a town of about 35,000 just north of Orlando.

Robinson was to play for Montreal, a Dodgers' organisation farm team with which he was preparing for the following year's "great experiment", when he would break the major league colour line with Brooklyn.
Sanford police chief Roy Williams was called to the ball park by a fan upset at Robinson's presence and the future Hall of Famer was led back to the dugout by police.

Williams later announced that Robinson would be allowed to work out with teammates at the park and play three innings per game. He did have to stay with a black family rather than at the team's hotel.
"I guess it was a compromise. Chief Williams was known sort of as a negotiator," Dale said, explaining what passed for enlightenment in the days of the segregated south.
Other towns across the Florida, traditional home of baseball's pre-season spring training camps, cancelled games rather than let Robinson play alongside white players.

Dale said city leaders had decided to apologise to Robinson's family and the Dodgers, now in Los Angeles, during a commission meeting Monday night. He said the town intended to send a letter and issue a proclamation, but had not yet been able to convey the formal apology.

Baseball marked the 50th anniversary of Robinson's major league debut with a celebration of his life at New York's Shea Stadium Tuesday night. The game was interrupted after the fifth inning for a special tribute led by President Bill Clinton and Robinson's widow Rachel.
Major League Baseball officially retired Robinson's uniform number 42 as part of the tribute.
